title: Beyond the dashboard: The high cost of fragmented poverty data
gist: Global poverty data sits in thematic silos that almost never sample the same households, so only two indicators are collected across all four major cross-national survey databases and the overlap between lack of electricity and any other deprivation is observable for under 8 percent of the world's population. The authors argue this invisibility causes ministries to duplicate procurement and fixed delivery costs, and that seeing overlaps would sometimes make an energy intervention the most cost-effective education policy.

insights.claim: The fragmentation of poverty data across separate datasets is not a technical inconvenience but a determinant of policy, because it shapes what governments can see and therefore what they act on.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Explains why development spending is often misallocated even where budgets are adequate, and why data-integration investments have outsized policy leverage.
insights.quote: Fragmented data leads to fragmented policies.

insights.claim: Some poverty dimensions are never measured at all because of budget constraints, conflict, or other barriers with no immediate solution, so gaps are structural rather than temporary.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Data blind spots cluster in the hardest environments, meaning the places with the greatest need have the least measurable evidence base to attract funding.
insights.locator: Poverty is multidimensional, but measuring it that way is not easy

insights.claim: The World Bank's Global Monitoring Database captures income or consumption plus basic demographics across more than 160 economies while the Demographic and Health Surveys capture demographic and health information for reproductive-age women and men across more than 90 economies, but the two almost never sample the same households, making it impossible to link individuals across surveys.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Non-overlapping sampling frames, not access alone, are the binding constraint on multidimensional poverty measurement, which is why statistical matching methods matter.
insights.locator: The fragmented landscape of poverty data

insights.claim: Only two indicators, educational attainment and phone ownership, are collected across all four major cross-national survey databases: EU-SILC, the Gallup World Poll, DHS/MICS, and SEDLAC.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Phone ownership and education are the only globally comparable non-income indicators available today, which explains their outsized role in development proxies and targeting.
insights.locator: A recent paper documents the gap

insights.claim: Although electricity access data appears in four of the five major databases in support of SDG 7, the overlap between lack of electricity access and any other deprivation can be observed for only 61 countries covered by Latin American data and EU-SILC, representing less than 8 percent of the global population.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Claims about energy poverty interacting with other deprivations are effectively unmeasurable for 92 percent of humanity, a caution for anyone citing global energy-poverty co-benefits.
insights.locator: To take one example, SDG 7 calls for universal access to electricity

themes.theme: Single versus dashboard versus overlap views

insights.claim: A dashboard view of poverty is actively misleading rather than merely incomplete, because it reports how many people face each problem individually while saying nothing about whether they are the same people facing multiple deprivations simultaneously.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A practical test for any indicator dashboard used in allocation decisions: if it cannot show joint distributions, it cannot support bundling or targeting choices.

insights.claim: In Angola's 2018 data, nearly 2 in 5 people lived on less than $3 a day in 2021 PPP terms, nearly 1 in 3 lacked adequate education, and more than 2 in 3 lacked basic infrastructure.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Concrete baseline showing infrastructure deprivation exceeding monetary poverty by a wide margin, which reorders which intervention has the largest addressable population.
insights.locator: Let's look at an example of single and multidimensional view

insights.claim: The multidimensional view of Angola reveals that nearly a fifth of the population faces income, education and infrastructure deprivation simultaneously, an overlap entirely invisible in either a single-dimension or dashboard presentation.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: A large concentrated triple-deprived group is exactly the population where bundled delivery generates the highest return per dollar.
insights.locator: A multidimensional view shows a more complete picture

insights.claim: Monetary poverty overlaps substantially with other forms of poverty and is a crucial starting point, but it does not capture all poor households on its own.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Income-only targeting systematically misses a portion of the deprived population, an argument for hybrid targeting in cash transfer and subsidy programs.
insights.locator: This is a crucial starting point

insights.claim: When deprivation overlaps are invisible, ministries act separately by hiring different contractors, running separate procurement processes and duplicating fixed delivery costs, whereas seeing the overlap enables bundled infrastructure, shared fixed costs and dig-once delivery that stretches the same investment across more households.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Identifies a concrete efficiency pool in development spending that better data can unlock, relevant to contractors and financiers who bid on bundled versus siloed programs.
insights.locator: Getting it wrong can be costly

insights.claim: The most cost-effective education policy might actually be an energy policy: if most children dropping out live in homes without electricity and cannot study after dark, or attend schools without power, connecting those households to the grid may do more for enrollment than building new classrooms.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: Cross-sector substitution effects mean sector-specific budget lines can be systematically misallocated, and electrification programs may deserve education-budget credit.

insights.claim: A recent paper highlighted in a companion blog introduces a method for combining aggregate statistics from fragmented datasets to measure multidimensional poverty even when individuals cannot be linked across surveys.
insights.speaker: World Bank Blogs
insights.so_what: If validated and adopted, this lets governments infer overlap without new surveys, which would be far cheaper than expanding data collection.
